00290 |    .. versionchanged:: 3.11
00291 |       Added the *context* parameter.
00292 | 
00293 | 
00294 | Task Cancellation
00295 | =================
00296 | 
00297 | Tasks can easily and safely be cancelled.
00298 | When a task is cancelled, :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError` will be raised
00299 | in the task at the next opportunity.
00300 | 
00301 | It is recommended that coroutines use ``try/finally`` blocks to robustly
00302 | perform clean-up logic. In case :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError`
00303 | is explicitly caught, it should generally be propagated when
00304 | clean-up is complete. :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError` directly subclasses
00305 | :exc:`BaseException` so most code will not need to be aware of it.
00306 | 
00307 | The asyncio components that enable structured concurrency, like
00308 | :class:`asyncio.TaskGroup` and :func:`asyncio.timeout`,
00309 | are implemented using cancellation internally and might misbehave if
00310 | a coroutine swallows :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError`. Similarly, user code
00311 | should not generally call :meth:`uncancel <asyncio.Task.uncancel>`.
00312 | However, in cases when suppressing :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError` is
00313 | truly desired, it is necessary to also call ``uncancel()`` to completely
00314 | remove the cancellation state.
00315 | 
00316 | .. _taskgroups:
00317 | 
00318 | Task Groups
00319 | ===========
00320 | 
00321 | Task groups combine a task creation API with a convenient
00322 | and reliable way to wait for all tasks in the group to finish.
00323 | 
00324 | .. class:: TaskGroup()
00325 | 
00326 |    An :ref:`asynchronous context manager <async-context-managers>`
00327 |    holding a group of tasks.
00328 |    Tasks can be added to the group using :meth:`create_task`.
00329 |    All tasks are awaited when the context manager exits.
00330 | 
00331 |    .. versionadded:: 3.11
00332 | 
00333 |    .. method:: create_task(coro, *, name=None, context=None)
00334 | 
00335 |       Create a task in this task group.
00336 |       The signature matches that of :func:`asyncio.create_task`.
00337 |       If the task group is inactive (e.g. not yet entered,
00338 |       already finished, or in the process of shutting down),
00339 |       we will close the given ``coro``.
00340 | 
00341 |       .. versionchanged:: 3.13
00342 | 
00343 |          Close the given coroutine if the task group is not active.
00344 | 
00345 | Example::
00346 | 
00347 |     async def main():
00348 |         async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
00349 |             task1 = tg.create_task(some_coro(...))
00350 |             task2 = tg.create_task(another_coro(...))
00351 |         print(f"Both tasks have completed now: {task1.result()}, {task2.result()}")
00352 | 
00353 | The ``async with`` statement will wait for all tasks in the group to finish.
00354 | While waiting, new tasks may still be added to the group
00355 | (for example, by passing ``tg`` into one of the coroutines
00356 | and calling ``tg.create_task()`` in that coroutine).
00357 | Once the last task has finished and the ``async with`` block is exited,
00358 | no new tasks may be added to the group.
00359 | 
00360 | The first time any of the tasks belonging to the group fails
00361 | with an exception other than :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError`,
00362 | the remaining tasks in the group are cancelled.
00363 | No further tasks can then be added to the group.
00364 | At this point, if the body of the ``async with`` statement is still active
00365 | (i.e., :meth:`~object.__aexit__` hasn't been called yet),
00366 | the task directly containing the ``async with`` statement is also cancelled.
00367 | The resulting :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError` will interrupt an ``await``,
00368 | but it will not bubble out of the containing ``async with`` statement.
00369 | 
00370 | Once all tasks have finished, if any tasks have failed
00371 | with an exception other than :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError`,
00372 | those exceptions are combined in an
00373 | :exc:`ExceptionGroup` or :exc:`BaseExceptionGroup`
00374 | (as appropriate; see their documentation)
00375 | which is then raised.
00376 | 
00377 | Two base exceptions are treated specially:
00378 | If any task fails with :exc:`KeyboardInterrupt` or :exc:`SystemExit`,
00379 | the task group still cancels the remaining tasks and waits for them,
00380 | but then the initial :exc:`KeyboardInterrupt` or :exc:`SystemExit`
00381 | is re-raised instead of :exc:`ExceptionGroup` or :exc:`BaseExceptionGroup`.
00382 | 
00383 | If the body of the ``async with`` statement exits with an exception
00384 | (so :meth:`~object.__aexit__` is called with an exception set),
00385 | this is treated the same as if one of the tasks failed:
00386 | the remaining tasks are cancelled and then waited for,
00387 | and non-cancellation exceptions are grouped into an
00388 | exception group and raised.
00389 | The exception passed into :meth:`~object.__aexit__`,
00390 | unless it is :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError`,
00391 | is also included in the exception group.
00392 | The same special case is made for
00393 | :exc:`KeyboardInterrupt` and :exc:`SystemExit` as in the previous paragraph.
00394 | 
00395 | Task groups are careful not to mix up the internal cancellation used to
00396 | "wake up" their :meth:`~object.__aexit__` with cancellation requests
00397 | for the task in which they are running made by other parties.
00398 | In particular, when one task group is syntactically nested in another,
00399 | and both experience an exception in one of their child tasks simultaneously,
00400 | the inner task group will process its exceptions, and then the outer task group
00401 | will receive another cancellation and process its own exceptions.
00402 | 
00403 | In the case where a task group is cancelled externally and also must
00404 | raise an :exc:`ExceptionGroup`, it will call the parent task's
00405 | :meth:`~asyncio.Task.cancel` method. This ensures that a
00406 | :exc:`asyncio.CancelledError` will be raised at the next
00407 | :keyword:`await`, so the cancellation is not lost.
00408 | 
00409 | Task groups preserve the cancellation count
00410 | reported by :meth:`asyncio.Task.cancelling`.
00411 | 
00412 | .. versionchanged:: 3.13
00413 | 
00414 |    Improved handling of simultaneous internal and external cancellations
00415 |    and correct preservation of cancellation counts.
00416 | 

00508 | Running Tasks Concurrently
00509 | ==========================
00510 | 
00511 | .. awaitablefunction:: gather(*aws, return_exceptions=False)
00512 | 
00513 |    Run :ref:`awaitable objects <asyncio-awaitables>` in the *aws*
00514 |    sequence *concurrently*.
00515 | 
00516 |    If any awaitable in *aws* is a coroutine, it is automatically
00517 |    scheduled as a Task.
00518 | 
00519 |    If all awaitables are completed successfully, the result is an
00520 |    aggregate list of returned values.  The order of result values
00521 |    corresponds to the order of awaitables in *aws*.
00522 | 
00523 |    If *return_exceptions* is ``False`` (default), the first
00524 |    raised exception is immediately propagated to the task that
00525 |    awaits on ``gather()``.  Other awaitables in the *aws* sequence
00526 |    **won't be cancelled** and will continue to run.
00527 | 
00528 |    If *return_exceptions* is ``True``, exceptions are treated the
00529 |    same as successful results, and aggregated in the result list.
00530 | 
00531 |    If ``gather()`` is *cancelled*, all submitted awaitables
00532 |    (that have not completed yet) are also *cancelled*.
00533 | 
00534 |    If any Task or Future from the *aws* sequence is *cancelled*, it is
00535 |    treated as if it raised :exc:`CancelledError` -- the ``gather()``
00536 |    call is **not** cancelled in this case.  This is to prevent the
00537 |    cancellation of one submitted Task/Future to cause other
00538 |    Tasks/Futures to be cancelled.
00539 | 
00540 |    .. note::
00541 |       A new alternative to create and run tasks concurrently and
00542 |       wait for their completion is :class:`asyncio.TaskGroup`. *TaskGroup*
00543 |       provides stronger safety guarantees than *gather* for scheduling a nesting of subtasks:
00544 |       if a task (or a subtask, a task scheduled by a task)
00545 |       raises an exception, *TaskGroup* will, while *gather* will not,
00546 |       cancel the remaining scheduled tasks).
00547 | 
00548 |    .. _asyncio_example_gather:
00549 | 
00550 |    Example::
00551 | 
00552 |       import asyncio
00553 | 
00554 |       async def factorial(name, number):
00555 |           f = 1
00556 |           for i in range(2, number + 1):
00557 |               print(f"Task {name}: Compute factorial({number}), currently i={i}...")
00558 |               await asyncio.sleep(1)
00559 |               f *= i
00560 |           print(f"Task {name}: factorial({number}) = {f}")
00561 |           return f
00562 | 
00563 |       async def main():
00564 |           # Schedule three calls *concurrently*:
00565 |           L = await asyncio.gather(
00566 |               factorial("A", 2),
00567 |               factorial("B", 3),
00568 |               factorial("C", 4),
00569 |           )
00570 |           print(L)
00571 | 
00572 |       asyncio.run(main())
00573 | 
00574 |       # Expected output:
00575 |       #
00576 |       #     Task A: Compute factorial(2), currently i=2...
00577 |       #     Task B: Compute factorial(3), currently i=2...
00578 |       #     Task C: Compute factorial(4), currently i=2...
00579 |       #     Task A: factorial(2) = 2
00580 |       #     Task B: Compute factorial(3), currently i=3...
00581 |       #     Task C: Compute factorial(4), currently i=3...
00582 |       #     Task B: factorial(3) = 6
00583 |       #     Task C: Compute factorial(4), currently i=4...
00584 |       #     Task C: factorial(4) = 24
00585 |       #     [2, 6, 24]
00586 | 
00587 |    .. note::
00588 |       If *return_exceptions* is false, cancelling gather() after it
00589 |       has been marked done won't cancel any submitted awaitables.
00590 |       For instance, gather can be marked done after propagating an
00591 |       exception to the caller, therefore, calling ``gather.cancel()``
00592 |       after catching an exception (raised by one of the awaitables) from
00593 |       gather won't cancel any other awaitables.
00594 | 
00595 |    .. versionchanged:: 3.7
00596 |       If the *gather* itself is cancelled, the cancellation is
00597 |       propagated regardless of *return_exceptions*.
00598 | 
00599 |    .. versionchanged:: 3.10

02129 | .. _sqlite3-connection-context-manager:
02130 | 
02131 | How to use the connection context manager
02132 | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
02133 | 
02134 | A :class:`Connection` object can be used as a context manager that
02135 | automatically commits or rolls back open transactions when leaving the body of
02136 | the context manager.
02137 | If the body of the :keyword:`with` statement finishes without exceptions,
02138 | the transaction is committed.
02139 | If this commit fails,
02140 | or if the body of the ``with`` statement raises an uncaught exception,
02141 | the transaction is rolled back.
02142 | 
02143 | If there is no open transaction upon leaving the body of the ``with`` statement,
02144 | the context manager is a no-op.
02145 | 
02146 | .. note::
02147 | 
02148 |    The context manager neither implicitly opens a new transaction
02149 |    nor closes the connection.
02150 | 
02151 | .. testcode::
02152 | 
02153 |    con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
02154 |    con.execute("CREATE TABLE lang(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR UNIQUE)")
02155 | 
02156 |    # Successful, con.commit() is called automatically afterwards
02157 |    with con:
02158 |        con.execute("INSERT INTO lang(name) VALUES(?)", ("Python",))
02159 | 
02160 |    # con.rollback() is called after the with block finishes with an exception,
02161 |    # the exception is still raised and must be caught
02162 |    try:
02163 |        with con:
02164 |            con.execute("INSERT INTO lang(name) VALUES(?)", ("Python",))
02165 |    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
02166 |        print("couldn't add Python twice")
02167 | 
02168 |    # Connection object used as context manager only commits or rollbacks transactions,
02169 |    # so the connection object should be closed manually
02170 |    con.close()
02171 | 
02172 | .. testoutput::
02173 |    :hide:
02174 | 
02175 |    couldn't add Python twice

02398 | How to use the connection context manager
02399 | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
02400 | 
02401 | A :class:`Connection` object can be used as a context manager that
02402 | automatically commits or rolls back open transactions when leaving the body of
02403 | the context manager.
02404 | If the body of the :keyword:`with` statement finishes without exceptions,
02405 | the transaction is committed.
02406 | If this commit fails,
02407 | or if the body of the ``with`` statement raises an uncaught exception,
02408 | the transaction is rolled back.
02409 | If :attr:`~Connection.autocommit` is ``False``,
02410 | a new transaction is implicitly opened after committing or rolling back.

02413 | or if :attr:`~Connection.autocommit` is ``True``,
02414 | the context manager does nothing.

02418 |    nor closes the connection. If you need a closing context manager, consider
02419 |    using :meth:`contextlib.closing`.

02645 | Transaction control
02646 | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
02647 | 
02648 | :mod:`!sqlite3` offers multiple methods of controlling whether,
02649 | when and how database transactions are opened and closed.
02650 | :ref:`sqlite3-transaction-control-autocommit` is recommended,

02655 | 
02656 | Transaction control via the ``autocommit`` attribute
02657 | """"""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""
02658 | 
02659 | The recommended way of controlling transaction behaviour is through
02660 | the :attr:`Connection.autocommit` attribute,
02661 | which should preferably be set using the *autocommit* parameter
02662 | of :func:`connect`.
02663 | 
02664 | It is suggested to set *autocommit* to ``False``,
02665 | which implies :pep:`249`-compliant transaction control.
02666 | This means:
02667 | 
02668 | * :mod:`!sqlite3` ensures that a transaction is always open,
02669 |   so :func:`connect`, :meth:`Connection.commit`, and :meth:`Connection.rollback`
02670 |   will implicitly open a new transaction
02671 |   (immediately after closing the pending one, for the latter two).
02672 |   :mod:`!sqlite3` uses ``BEGIN DEFERRED`` statements when opening transactions.
02673 | * Transactions should be committed explicitly using :meth:`!commit`.
02674 | * Transactions should be rolled back explicitly using :meth:`!rollback`.
02675 | * An implicit rollback is performed if the database is
02676 |   :meth:`~Connection.close`-ed with pending changes.
02677 | 
02678 | Set *autocommit* to ``True`` to enable SQLite's `autocommit mode`_.
02679 | In this mode, :meth:`Connection.commit` and :meth:`Connection.rollback`
02680 | have no effect.
02681 | Note that SQLite's autocommit mode is distinct from
02682 | the :pep:`249`-compliant :attr:`Connection.autocommit` attribute;
02683 | use :attr:`Connection.in_transaction` to query
02684 | the low-level SQLite autocommit mode.
02685 | 
02686 | Set *autocommit* to :data:`LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL`
02687 | to leave transaction control behaviour to the
02688 | :attr:`Connection.isolation_level` attribute.
02689 | See :ref:`sqlite3-transaction-control-isolation-level` for more information.

Original source line numbers follow.

00600 |    <para>
00601 |     Creating an index can interfere with regular operation of a database.
00602 |     Normally <productname>PostgreSQL</productname> locks the table to be indexed against
00603 |     writes and performs the entire index build with a single scan of the
00604 |     table. Other transactions can still read the table, but if they try to
00605 |     insert, update, or delete rows in the table they will block until the
00606 |     index build is finished. This could have a severe effect if the system is
00607 |     a live production database.  Very large tables can take many hours to be
00608 |     indexed, and even for smaller tables, an index build can lock out writers
00609 |     for periods that are unacceptably long for a production system.
00610 |    </para>
00611 | 
00612 |    <para>
00613 |     <productname>PostgreSQL</productname> supports building indexes without locking
00614 |     out writes.  This method is invoked by specifying the
00615 |     <literal>CONCURRENTLY</literal> option of <command>CREATE INDEX</command>.
00616 |     When this option is used,
00617 |     <productname>PostgreSQL</productname> must perform two scans of the table, and in
00618 |     addition it must wait for all existing transactions that could potentially
00619 |     modify or use the index to terminate.  Thus
00620 |     this method requires more total work than a standard index build and takes
00621 |     significantly longer to complete.  However, since it allows normal
00622 |     operations to continue while the index is built, this method is useful for
00623 |     adding new indexes in a production environment.  Of course, the extra CPU
00624 |     and I/O load imposed by the index creation might slow other operations.
00625 |    </para>
00626 | 
00627 |    <para>
00628 |     In a concurrent index build, the index is actually entered as an
00629 |     <quote>invalid</quote> index into
00630 |     the system catalogs in one transaction, then two table scans occur in
00631 |     two more transactions.  Before each table scan, the index build must
00632 |     wait for existing transactions that have modified the table to terminate.
00633 |     After the second scan, the index build must wait for any transactions
00634 |     that have a snapshot (see <xref linkend="mvcc"/>) predating the second
00635 |     scan to terminate, including transactions used by any phase of concurrent
00636 |     index builds on other tables, if the indexes involved are partial or have
00637 |     columns that are not simple column references.
00638 |     Then finally the index can be marked <quote>valid</quote> and ready for use,
00639 |     and the <command>CREATE INDEX</command> command terminates.
00640 |     Even then, however, the index may not be immediately usable for queries:
00641 |     in the worst case, it cannot be used as long as transactions exist that
00642 |     predate the start of the index build.
00643 |    </para>
00644 | 
00645 |    <para>
00646 |     If a problem arises while scanning the table, such as a deadlock or a
00647 |     uniqueness violation in a unique index, the <command>CREATE INDEX</command>
00648 |     command will fail but leave behind an <quote>invalid</quote> index. This index
00649 |     will be ignored for querying purposes because it might be incomplete;
00650 |     however it will still consume update overhead. The <application>psql</application>
00651 |     <command>\d</command> command will report such an index as <literal>INVALID</literal>:
00652 | 
00653 | <programlisting>
00654 | postgres=# \d tab
00655 |        Table "public.tab"
00656 |  Column |  Type   | Collation | Nullable | Default
00657 | --------+---------+-----------+----------+---------
00658 |  col    | integer |           |          |
00659 | Indexes:
00660 |     "idx" btree (col) INVALID
00661 | </programlisting>
00662 | 
00663 |     The recommended recovery
00664 |     method in such cases is to drop the index and try again to perform
00665 |     <command>CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY</command>.  (Another possibility is
00666 |     to rebuild the index with <command>REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY</command>).
00667 |    </para>
00668 | 
00669 |    <para>
00670 |     Another caveat when building a unique index concurrently is that the
00671 |     uniqueness constraint is already being enforced against other transactions
00672 |     when the second table scan begins.  This means that constraint violations
00673 |     could be reported in other queries prior to the index becoming available
00674 |     for use, or even in cases where the index build eventually fails.  Also,
00675 |     if a failure does occur in the second scan, the <quote>invalid</quote> index
00676 |     continues to enforce its uniqueness constraint afterwards.
00677 |    </para>
00678 | 
00679 |    <para>
00680 |     Concurrent builds of expression indexes and partial indexes are supported.
00681 |     Errors occurring in the evaluation of these expressions could cause
00682 |     behavior similar to that described above for unique constraint violations.
00683 |    </para>
00684 | 
00685 |    <para>
00686 |     Regular index builds permit other regular index builds on the
00687 |     same table to occur simultaneously, but only one concurrent index build
00688 |     can occur on a table at a time.  In either case, schema modification of the
00689 |     table is not allowed while the index is being built.  Another difference is
00690 |     that a regular <command>CREATE INDEX</command> command can be performed
00691 |     within a transaction block, but <command>CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY</command>
00692 |     cannot.
00693 |    </para>
00694 | 
00695 |    <para>
00696 |     Concurrent builds for indexes on partitioned tables are currently not
00697 |     supported.  However, you may concurrently build the index on each
00698 |     partition individually and then finally create the partitioned index
00699 |     non-concurrently in order to reduce the time where writes to the
00700 |     partitioned table will be locked out.  In this case, building the
00701 |     partitioned index is a metadata only operation.
00702 |    </para>
